“How do you generate SP so fast?”

me : “Skill injectors baby, but why?”

My char: One Ugly Cat

Got asked in-game how I trained up so fast. Fair question, so here’s the honest answer: I’m a returning vet, played the conventional way years back, joined corps, followed the cookie-cutter roadmaps, ground out skill queues and ISK the slow way. It cost me huge amounts of time and money, and I could never actually specialize, because every choice meant trading off something else I needed. Getting blown up after hours of grinding isn’t character building, it’s just fatigue.

This time around I asked myself, if I could buy back all that wasted time, would I? Yes, instantly. So I did. Bought PLEX, converted to skill injectors and books, filled in exactly the skills I wanted maxed, no drama. That’s not dishonorable, it’s just recognizing the game already runs on a pay-to-progress model whether you admit it or not. I’d rather spend money once and actually play the game I want, than spend months not playing it at all.

Everyone wants the flashy skills first, the big guns, the titans, the fancy ships. But here’s the secret nobody tells new players. If you want to actually get rich in this game, train Accounting and Broker Relations to level five before almost anything else.

Every single time you buy or sell on the market, CCP takes a cut, sales tax on the way out, broker fees on the way in. Untrained, you’re bleeding a chunk of every transaction straight into the void. Multiply that by every ship, every module, every skill injector you’ll ever trade over your whole EVE career, and that’s real wealth you’re just giving away for free.

Two skill books, one modest chunk of skill points, and suddenly you’re keeping more of everything you touch, forever. It’s the most boring investment in the game and also the highest return one. Train it once, profit from it every single day after.

And if you really want to squeeze every drop out of this, don’t even use your main. Roll a trading alt through a referral link, that gets you a free chunk of starter skill points right out of the gate, throw a couple of cheap skill injectors at it, and train Trade, Accounting, and Broker Relations to five on that character alone. Now every single trade you ever make runs through the cheapest possible tax rate, forever, without touching your main’s skill plan at all.

I just don’t see yet how keeping the characters limited in SP is going to help.

The key is skill injector efficiency. Once a character passes 50M SP, injectors give you less skill points per injector, and it gets worse again past 80M. That penalty hits hard when you’re paying real money to inject. So if you’re skill injecting, going past 50M on one character is just burning cash for diminishing returns.

The solution is 3 focused modular characters, all flying the Legion, all kept under fifty million skill points. One is your armor and laser fit, another is your shield and missile fit, and so on. Each one is highly proficient within its specialty, and you simply swap between them depending on the situation without ever gimping yourself.

This approach only really matters if you’re injecting. If you’re training the old fashioned way, time is your only cost and eventually you hit everything anyway. But for anyone who wants to immediately fly an optimized focused character and is paying to do it, keeping each alt under 50M and staying modular is the most cost efficient way to build serious combat flexibility fast.

Limitations

  • You need a minimum of 5,500,000 skillpoints to use an extractor (can’t drop below 5 million skillpoints).
  • A single extractor holds 500,000 skillpoints (500k) and the total worth of skillspoints for the skills you select must equal to or exceed this number in order to create a Skill Injector.
    • You cannot extract skillpoints from a skill that is a prerequisite for another skill, so if you want to get rid of a whole chain of skills you’ll need to extract the skills from the top down.
  • If the account to be extracted from is in Alpha Clone State, characters may only extract skills requiring Omega Clone State.
  • Certain skills cannot be removed, such as:
    • Infomorph Psychology
    • Advanced Infomorph Psychology
    • Cybernetics
    • Command Center Upgrades
    • Interplanetary Consolidation

Strength in numbers

EVE-Online-Legion-Art-1200x9001200×900 109 KB

This game runs on a hidden tax, and that tax is compromise. Every ship class, from your starter frigate all the way to a strategic cruiser, is deliberately gated behind a wall of skills, modules, and fleet dependency that makes solo competence nearly impossible without paying one of three currencies, time, isk grinding, or real dollars.

The lore sells you on being a lone space pirate, but the mechanics quietly funnel you into fleets and support roles instead, because that’s where the game actually functions smoothly for its design. Copying a proficient solo pilot’s exact fit and playstyle is completely achievable in a week, not years, if you’re willing to pay real money to skip the grind, the years everyone else spent are not skill, they’re just time debt.

The real goal isn’t slowly earning your stripes, it’s calculating your build to a plateau, maxing every relevant skill to level five, until nobody can out-fit you on paper, at which point the fights become a chess match you’ve already won before undocking. Once you hit that plateau, you stop compromising and start actually playing, everything before that point was just the tax.

Ghost Recon Solo PVP Legion

Now here’s the part that really exposes the game’s design, solo play against the entrenched power structures is nearly impossible by intention, not by accident.

Take Goonswarm, strip away their coalition, their intel network, their sovereignty, and their numbers, and they’re just individual pilots with nothing special. Their actual power comes entirely from insulation, they rarely lose anything that matters because the system is rigged in their favor before the fight even starts. A battleship sitting safely in friendly null sec with officer modules and full intel coverage is functionally unkillable to a lone cruiser, not because that pilot is skilled, but because the entire environment around him guarantees he never has to prove it.

Example of a solo pvp’er guaranteeing his wins

We are Legion

So here’s my actual project, can solo play still be fun against that kind of stacked deck? My answer is yes, but only if you stop trying to fight fair. A strategic cruiser, specifically the Legion, is my answer, cloaked, mobile, and completely untethered from any alliance’s protection or obligation, meaning nobody can predict where I’ll strike or when I’ll vanish. I’m not trying to out-tank the system, I’m trying to be the one variable it never accounted for.

The setup itself is where the actual engineering happens. I’m running a triple character configuration, one Legion built for pure alpha strike damage, and a second character sitting in a stripped down Legion whose only job is cloaking and firing command bursts, no tank, no weapons, nothing but leadership skills, because skill extraction taught me that specialization only matters where it’s actually used. That booster ship gives my combat Legion a serious damage and speed multiplier the moment I decloak, meaning fights are decided in seconds, not the slow three minute shield-to-armor-to-hull grind you see in most solo PvP videos.

My base of operations won’t be a station or even null sec territory at all, it’ll be a wormhole, appearing and disappearing on its own natural cycle, giving me an untraceable staging point with zero footprint anyone can scout or camp. The whole loop is scout, study patterns, strike fast, and vanish back through the hole before local even catches up, and every single episode gets held back and released on a long delay specifically so nobody can use my own footage against my current position or tactics. This is the actual test of whether solo play can still be fun in this game, not whether I can win every fight, but whether I can build something clever enough that the house’s usual advantages simply don’t apply to me.
